title: Valuation Expo 2026: What It Meant for ValueMate
summary: We arrived in Las Vegas ready to launch ValueMate Studio. We left with a clearer sense of what appraisers need—and how much demand there is for a better way to work.
body_markdown:
Valuation Expo 2026 was not simply another conference for us. It was the moment we had chosen to introduce ValueMate Studio beyond our own appraisal firm.


For months, the dates had been fixed on our calendar: August 16 through 19 at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. We had committed to attend as a diamond sponsor. Anir and Scott were scheduled to speak. Our booth, meeting room, demonstrations, and launch plans were all in motion.


We arrived with a product that had already been shaped by live UAD 3.6 assignments inside VM Appraisals. The conference was our opportunity to show the broader industry what that approach had made possible.


## Building toward the week


ValueMate Studio began as an internal tool for VM Appraisals. Our appraisers were among the first to complete assignments under the new standard, and the available software was making the transition harder than it needed to be. We built our own system because our firm needed one that could work reliably in production.


Once we saw how much it changed the process, we decided to make it available to other appraisers. Valuation Expo became the natural place to introduce it publicly.


By the time of the conference, GSE verification was complete and appraisers could create an account and begin using the software themselves. The focus of the week was no longer internal development. It was putting ValueMate Studio in front of appraisers and letting them experience the full workflow.


On Saturday, August 15, the team was inside Caesars Palace assembling the booth. By the next day, appraisers were arriving and ValueMate Studio was ready for its public debut.


## Showing the product in the open


There is a useful honesty to demonstrating software in front of the people who do the work every day. Appraisers know where a workflow breaks. They know which details matter, which shortcuts create problems later, and whether a new tool actually understands the assignment.


We were presenting an idea that had not been demonstrated at this scale before: an appraiser could move through the complete UAD 3.6 workflow and produce a finished report in record time, without giving up control of the analysis or the final opinion of value.


Vivek started the morning's mobile technology program with a live demonstration of ValueMate Studio on the main conference stage. Appraisers could see that idea working as a complete system, from capturing a property in the field to producing the UAD 3.6 report.


The following day, Anir and Scott took the main stage for a VET Talk titled “The Competitive Edge: Technology and the Future of Valuation.” Their perspectives came from two sides of the same company. Anir spoke as the founder building the technology; Scott spoke as a career appraiser who had spent decades finding better ways to produce credible work. Together, they made the case that technology is most useful when it strengthens the appraiser's judgment instead of trying to work around it.


That was also the idea behind our presence at the conference. ValueMate and VM Appraisals shared one booth because the software and the firm are part of the same learning loop. Our appraisers use what we build on real assignments. Their experience shapes the product, and the product gives the firm new ways to operate.


## More than a booth


The booth stayed packed throughout the conference. Some people came after seeing the mobile demonstration or the VET Talk. Others had heard about ValueMate Studio from another appraiser and wanted to see it for themselves. Many arrived with a specific problem from an active UAD 3.6 assignment—and they wanted to walk through the product in detail.


We had six people giving live demonstrations at the booth from morning until night. Appraisers wanted to see how ValueMate Studio handled inspections, data entry, comparable selection, validation, and revisions. They asked detailed questions and challenged us with the edge cases that only emerge from years in the field.


In addition to the continuous booth demonstrations, we held multiple group demos throughout the conference in our private meeting room. Those sessions were packed with appraisers looking for a more complete walkthrough, and the conversations often continued well beyond their allotted time. The volume was demanding, but it was also exactly what we had hoped for: direct feedback from the people the product was built to serve.


Away from the conference floor, we hosted an evening at F1 Arcade. Two hundred appraisers signed up to attend. It gave everyone room to talk without a screen or a presentation between us. Some conversations were about UAD 3.6 and software; others were simply about the profession, the businesses people had built, and what they wanted the next several years of appraisal work to look like.


Those informal conversations were as valuable as anything that happened on stage. A product can be demonstrated in twenty minutes. Trust takes longer, and it is built by listening.


## What came home with us


The immediate response exceeded our expectations. Roughly 300 appraisers signed up during the week after launch, not including enterprise users. New accounts were arriving at a rate of about 25 per day. Our calendar was booked two weeks out, with as many as 15 demonstrations taking place in a day.


The event also opened a different set of conversations. Major appraisal management companies expressed interest in piloting the product with their appraiser panels. Lenders wanted to understand what an AI-native appraisal workflow could mean for quality, consistency, and turnaround time. Those discussions are still developing, but they made clear that the need extends beyond an individual appraiser's desktop.


After the conference, the challenge became meeting the demand we had encountered: helping new users learn the product, supporting enterprise testing, and turning what we had demonstrated in person into useful videos and online guidance.


That is a much better problem to have.


## A beginning, not a finish line


Valuation Expo gave us evidence that the industry's appetite for better software is real. More importantly, it gave us hundreds of conversations about what “better” should mean.


Appraisers do not need technology that makes large promises from a distance. They need tools that respect the complexity of the work, survive real assignments, and give them more time for the analysis that requires their expertise. That is why we built ValueMate Studio alongside an appraisal firm, and why showing it to the industry in person mattered so much.


We went to Las Vegas to introduce ValueMate Studio publicly. We came home with new users, potential partners, a long list of ideas, and a larger responsibility to deliver on the interest we had seen.


Valuation Expo was the public beginning of this chapter for ValueMate. The work that follows is how we intend to earn it.
